graphMathHelp.title: How the graph thinks
graphMathHelp.subtitle: Every number on a node comes from a formula. Here's each one.
graphMathHelp.ownExplanation3: . A finished hard task contributes more to a goal's percentage than a finished easy one. If a goal has no tasks, its
graphMathHelp.ownExplanation5: progress is 0 by definition. Completion has to come from somewhere upstream.
graphMathHelp.ownExample: Three tasks: difficulty 1 (done), 2 (done), 3 (not done). Total weight = 6, completed weight = 3.
graphMathHelp.depsExplanation1: An incoming connection means "this goal's success depends on that one's." Edge weights say
graphMathHelp.depsExplanation3: . Dependency progress is the weighted average of every predecessor's
graphMathHelp.depsExplanation5: (so the calculation cascades all the way back through the graph).
graphMathHelp.depsExample: Goal A depends on B (weight 70, 80% complete) and C (weight 30, 50% complete).
graphMathHelp.totalFormula:
with own tasks:    total = own × 0.40 + deps × 0.60
without own tasks: total = own × 0.10 + deps × 0.90
graphMathHelp.totalExplanation1: When a goal has its own tasks, both numbers count, but dependencies still get the heavier vote (60%) because work doesn't happen in isolation. When a goal has
graphMathHelp.totalExplanation3: (a pure orchestration node, e.g., "Stay healthy"), it leans almost entirely on its dependencies. The clamp at the end keeps the result inside [0, 100].
graphMathHelp.importanceFormula:
avg = Σ(outgoingEdge.weight) / count(outgoingEdges)

Low      if no outgoing edges, OR avg ≤ 33.3
Medium   if 33.3 < avg < 66.6
High     if avg ≥ 66.6
graphMathHelp.importanceExplanation1: A goal's importance is read from how heavily
graphMathHelp.importanceExplanation3: . A goal with strong outgoing edges (averaging high weight) is a load-bearing column in your structure. A goal nothing depends on is just a leaf.
graphMathHelp.miniMapFormula:
red    if total < 33%
yellow if 33% ≤ total < 67%
green  if total ≥ 67%
graphMathHelp.miniMapExplanation1: The minimap in the bottom-right shades each node by its
graphMathHelp.miniMapExplanation3: so the cold spots are visible across the whole graph at once.
graphMathHelp.rationaleIntro: The graph treats goals as a network, not a list. Two ideas drive every formula above:
graphMathHelp.rationaleConnectionsBody: An edge says "this feeds that." Importance and dependency progress both fall out of the same edges; you only have to maintain one piece of structure.
graphMathHelp.rationaleDifficultyBody: Counting completed tasks alone treats a 10-minute errand the same as a multi-week project. Weighting by difficulty makes percentages mean something closer to actual effort.

self.attachmentSubtitle: What I want, and fear, when I'm close to someone.
self.loveGiveSubtitle: How I show care. Often diverges from how I best receive it.
self.loveReceiveSubtitle: What actually lands as love when someone offers it.
self.apologySubtitle: What I need to hear after harm, and what I default to giving.
self.conflictSubtitle: The mode I drop into when something goes sideways.
self.stressSubtitle: What my body does when I'm overloaded. Attachment is what I want; this is what I do.
self.releasedHelper: Releases, not regrets: stories, roles and expectations I no longer carry.
self.yearAheadTitle: What I want to be different in a year
self.yearAheadHelper: Concrete and observable. "Say no without explaining why," not "be more confident."
self.futureHelper: What you'd want them to know. Read this when you've forgotten.
self.attachmentSecureDesc: Comfortable with closeness and with distance. Trusts that needs can be expressed and met. Repairs after conflict. Can be alone without anxiety.
self.attachmentAnxiousDesc: Wants closeness, fears abandonment. Reads neutral signals as rejection. Pursues when a partner pulls away. Self-worth feels tied to the relationship's state.
self.attachmentAvoidantDesc: Values independence, uncomfortable with too much closeness. Pulls back when things get intense. Deactivates emotions; focuses on a partner's flaws when feeling vulnerable.
self.attachmentDisorganizedDesc: Wants closeness and fears it. Push-pull. Often comes from inconsistent or frightening early caregiving. Come here / go away.
self.loveActsDesc: Doing things: errands, fixing, lightening the load.
self.loveGiftsDesc: Tangible tokens of being thought of.
self.loveTouchDesc: Hugs, hand-holding, sitting close. Non-sexual touch counts most.
self.apologyRegretDesc: “I'm sorry I hurt you.” Naming the impact.
self.apologyResponsibilityDesc: “I was wrong.” No deflection, no excuses.
self.apologyRestitutionDesc: “How can I make this right?” Repair the harm.
self.apologyRepentingDesc: “I'll do this differently.” Naming the change.
self.apologyForgivenessDesc: “Will you forgive me?” Asking, not assuming.
self.conflictCompetingDesc: High assertiveness, low cooperation. Win the argument.
self.conflictAvoidingDesc: Low both. Step away and hope it dissolves.
self.conflictAccommodatingDesc: Low assertiveness, high cooperation. Yield to keep peace.
self.conflictCompromisingDesc: Middle on both. Each gives some; neither fully satisfied.
self.conflictCollaboratingDesc: High both. Widen the solution so both needs get met.
self.stressFawnDesc: Appease, caretake, suppress your own needs to keep the peace.

web.title: Pull one thread and the others move.
web.body1: A goal knows which values it answers to. A task can name the people it is for. A group like Family holds people and tasks at once. Each link you draw is another thread in the same web.
web.body2: Connections between goals carry a weight, and anansi works out which goals matter most from those weights. You never mark anything important. Tasks drift toward you on their own as their dates come closer.
web.name: The mark is Ananse Ntontan, the Adinkra symbol of the spider's web. It stands for wisdom, creativity and the complexity of life.
web.figureAria: The Ananse Ntontan web drawn large. Eight records hang on its outer ring: the goal Write the novel, the value Craft, the task Chapter two, the person Amara, a next bid about an essay, the date Papá turns 70, the group Family, and this week's Morning pages. Clay threads join the goal to its value, its task and the week; the task to Amara; Amara to her bid; and Family to Papá's date and to Amara.

claude.title: Talk to it through Claude.
claude.intro: anansi runs its own MCP server. Add it as a connector in Claude Desktop, Claude Code or claude.ai, approve once in your browser, and Claude can read and write your goals, people and Self page.
claude.how: Profile › Anansi for Claude has the URL and a ready .mcp.json snippet. Tokens belong to your account and can be revoked from your Claude client.
claude.transcriptAria: A conversation with Claude. You ask it to remind you to send Amara the essay you promised, by Sunday. Claude calls list_people, then create_next_bid, and answers that the bid is on Amara's page and on your Pulse. You ask what is coming up this month. Claude calls list_upcoming_next_bids and list_important_dates, and answers that Papá turns 70 in 11 days and that two bids are open, with Teo and with Lena.
claude.say1: Remind me to send Amara the essay I promised. By Sunday.
claude.reply1: Done. It's on Amara's page, and it shows on your Pulse under Upcoming.
claude.reply2: Papá turns 70 in 11 days. Two bids are open: ask Teo about the garden project, and book the cabin with Lena.

free.a: Nothing. anansi is free, with no paid tier and none planned.

access.q: How do I get an account?
access.a: With an invite code from someone who already has one. Every member has a personal code in their profile to share.

privacy.q: Who can read what I write?
privacy.a: You, and whoever administers the server. Traffic is encrypted in transit; the database is not encrypted at rest. The privacy page says exactly what is stored and where.

nudges.a: No. There are no notifications, no emails and no streaks. It is there when you open it.

export.q: Can I take my data with me?
export.a: Yes. Profile › Backups exports everything as one JSON file, attachments included, and the same file imports back.

claude.a: No. Everything works in the browser. Claude is one more way in.
